This is a layout sample, not a new published essay. It brings together the kinds of content a longer piece might need: a few sections, a photograph, a quotation, a table and a footnote. The aim is to keep the writing comfortable to read without making the page feel busy.

## Making space

A quiet page gives the eye somewhere to rest. The rhythm comes from paragraphs, useful headings and the occasional change of pace. ==An emphasis should earn its place==, rather than appearing simply because the design needs another colour.

Longer writing needs the same care as a short note. A paragraph should have enough room to develop a thought, while its line length should make it easy to find the beginning of the next line. On a small screen, the margins can shrink without letting the text become cramped.

> A useful interruption should leave you better able to return to what you were reading.

That applies to a link or an aside as much as it does to an illustration. A reader can follow a footnote and return to the same sentence.[^pace] There is no need for a permanent panel competing for attention beside the text.

## An illustration and its caption

![Matthew, used here to check image sizing](images/profile.jpg "An existing image, with a caption written in Markdown.")

Images stay within the reading column. A caption can explain why the image is here, while the alternative text describes it to someone who cannot see it. Neither needs to be an excuse for a large photographic header.

### A small comparison

Some ideas are easier to compare side by side. On a narrow screen this table scrolls within its own space, leaving the rest of the page in place.

| Piece | What it needs | What can stay optional |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A short note | A clear title and a few paragraphs | An introduction or illustration |
| A longer essay | Comfortable text and useful headings | Footnotes, tables and quotations |
| A review | Room for an opinion and its supporting detail | A photograph or a score |

> [!note] A quiet aside
> Callouts can carry an extra thought. They use the same restrained colours as the rest of the page, and can include ==a meaningful highlight== or **a little emphasis**.

## A practical example

A code sample should remain readable in both appearances. Obsidian markers inside code are examples, so they stay visible:

```js
const note = {
  title: 'A small observation',
  featured: true,
  featureOrder: 1,
};
// The strings "%% an example %%" and "==an example==" remain literal here.
```

There is a difference between showing `==highlight syntax==` and using ==**emphasis within a highlight**==. The first explains a convention; the second calls attention to the words themselves.

## Returning to the writing

The page ends as simply as it begins. A link offers another piece to read, but the reader can also stop here. A short note and a longer essay should feel like parts of the same site, with the amount of writing setting the pace.
